Methodology

Source: vignettes/articles/methodology.Rmd
methodology.Rmd

This article documents where howbig’s numbers come from: the simulated networks, how each method is scored, how the grid is used, and how the answers were checked.

Simulated networks

Each simulated design starts from two networks: group 1, and group 2, which equals group 1 plus a localized change.

Group 1 (default scenario) is built in four steps:

  1. Blocks. Features are split into blocks of 25 (designs with p < 50 use two equal blocks). Each block is a sparse Barabási-Albert tree (preferential attachment with one edge per new node).
  2. Between-block edges. Pairs in different blocks connect with probability 0.01 × 5 / B for B blocks, which keeps the expected number of between-block edges roughly constant as p grows.
  3. Edge weights. Weights are drawn from an empirical, metabolomics-derived distribution of partial correlations, excluding |weight| < 0.035.
  4. Precision matrix. Each off-diagonal entry is divided by 1.5 times its row’s absolute sum (Danaher et al. 2014), the diagonal is set to 1, and the diagonal is boosted if needed to make the matrix positive definite.

Group 2 applies one of three perturbations:

perturbation What changes Setting in the source study
"structural" All edges within block 1 are deleted A
"magnitude" Off-diagonal precision entries in block 1 are scaled by 1.5; no edges appear or disappear C
"both" Block 1 deleted and block 2 scaled by 1.5 B

Scaling is applied after the precision matrix is built, so the row-sum normalization cannot cancel it.

Ground truth. An edge is differential when the two groups’ precision entries differ by more than 0.01, i.e. |Θ₁ − Θ₂| > 0.01. This definition counts strength changes as well as edges that appear or disappear.

Data. Group 1 draws n₁ samples and group 2 draws n₂ samples from zero-mean multivariate normals with each group’s covariance (the inverse precision). Group 1 is the reference group, so with unequal groups the order of n = c(n1, n2) matters.

Differential edges are rare, and rarer as p grows

Because the change is confined to one or two blocks, the share of feature pairs that are truly differential falls sharply with p. That is the main reason designs with many features need large samples. Computed with the package’s own generator:

Features (p) Feature pairs Differential pairs (mean) Share differential
50 1225 40 3.27%
100 4950 46 0.93%
250 31125 52 0.17%
500 124750 51 0.04%

Assumption scenarios

At the anchor design (p = 100, n = 1000 per group, structural change) the grid also holds the same design under other assumptions, selected with scenario. Each shares the default design’s random seeds, so the comparison with the default is paired.

scenario What differs from the default
"scale_free" Denser Barabási-Albert blocks (two edges per new node; mean degree ~3.8, as in Danaher et al. 2014)
"erdos_renyi" Random blocks, within-block edge probability 0.15
"ar1_banded" No blocks: a banded network with geometrically decaying entries (ρ = 0.11, bandwidth 1); the change applies to features 1-25
"censored_5", "censored_25", "censored_50" Values below each feature’s detection limit set to zero, the limit chosen so about 5%, 25% or 50% of values are zero
"uniform_weights" Edge weights uniform on [−0.4, −0.1] ∪ [0.1, 0.4]

Methods

howbig includes the nine methods from the source study whose FDR-controlled calls could be scored across the grid. Each runs with the fixed configuration it had there:

Method Package Configuration How differential edges are called
JGL_BIC JGL Fused penalty; λ₁ then λ₂ chosen by BIC over a data-adaptive 10-value grid Permutation null + BH
JGL_BIC_GGL JGL Group penalty; same tuning Permutation null + BH
SSJGL spikeyglass Fused spike-and-slab; 3-step v₀ ladder Permutation null + BH
SSJGL_GGL spikeyglass Group spike-and-slab; same ladder Permutation null + BH
multiGGM multiGGM SSVS; 2 chains × (5,000 burn-in + 1,000 saved) Posterior FDR
InvCov (base R) Inverse sample covariance (pseudoinverse when singular) Permutation null + BH
mGHS multiGGM Multiple graphical horseshoe; 10,000 iterations, 5,000 burn-in Posterior FDR
DiffNetFDR DiffNetFDR Partial-correlation difference test The method’s own FDR procedure
ONDSA ONDSA / FastGGM Debiased differential test; λ = √(2 log(p / √n) / n) The method’s own FDR procedure

Seven further methods from the source study are not included: JRF (its sensitivity could be scored in under half the designs, and its differential score breaks down with unequal group sizes), jewel (it misses its FDR target, 0.13 at the anchor), D-trace and PNJGL (no FDR-controlled calls, so no power), and three sensitivity-check configurations run in only a few designs.

Scoring

FDR-controlled calls. Power needs a set of edges each method declares differential at the FDR target:

  • Permutation null + BH. One representative network pair is generated. For each of n_perm permutations, fresh data are drawn, group labels are shuffled (keeping the group sizes), and the method is refit. The edge scores |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂| from all permutations are pooled into one null distribution. Each observed edge score gets an empirical p-value against the pooled null, and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure is applied at the target.
  • Posterior FDR (Bayesian methods). Each edge gets its posterior probability that the two groups differ by more than 0.1, P(|Θ₁ − Θ₂| > 0.1). The largest top set of edges whose average (1 − probability) stays at or below the target is declared.
  • The method’s own FDR procedure. DiffNetFDR and ONDSA make their own calls at the target, and those are scored as they are.

From those calls:

  • Sensitivity (power) = true differential edges declared / all true differential edges.
  • Achieved FDR = declared edges that are not truly differential / all declared edges.
  • AUPR, a threshold-free secondary measure: area under the precision-recall curve of the method’s edge ranking.

Each replicate draws a fresh network and data. The reported value is the mean over replicates, with the 10th-90th percentile band showing how much power varies between networks.

The grid

The precomputed grid (100 replicates in 197 of its 206 cells) holds, for the default scenario:

  • sample-size arm: n = 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000 at p = 250;
  • feature arm: p = 50, 100, 200, 250, 300, 500 at n = 1000;
  • small samples at p = 100: n = 50 and 100;
  • the anchor (p = 100, n = 1000): all three perturbation types, unequal groups (n₁ = 500, n₂ = 1500, the same total), and the assumption scenarios above.

A few cells have fewer replicates because some fits failed or timed out; the thinnest (multiGGM at p = 500, n = 1000) has only 2, and howbig flags any cell with fewer than 20.

Interpolation

Queries on an arm, between grid points, are interpolated with a monotone (Fritsch-Carlson) spline on log(n) or log(p). Interpolation never extrapolates past the ends of an arm, never crosses between arms, and is never applied to unequal groups or non-default scenarios, which are answered exactly or not at all.

That restriction is deliberate and was tested:

Check Result
Leave-one-out along the feature arm mean absolute error 0.014 (sensitivity), 0.009 (AUPR)
Leave-one-out along the sample-size arm 0.018 (sensitivity), 0.014 (AUPR); worst case 0.06 (InvCov, whose curve bends sharply near n = 100)
Predicting an off-arm cell by combining the two arms (earlier grid) errors around 0.20, consistently too optimistic
Interpolated vs freshly simulated, p = 150, n = 1000, JGL_BIC sensitivity 0.65 vs 0.65 (± 0.02)
Unequal groups vs balanced groups at the harmonic-mean size not interchangeable: 0.61 vs 0.65 for JGL_BIC, 0.31 vs 0.39 for InvCov

So on-arm interpolation is trustworthy, while combining arms, or converting unequal groups to an “effective” balanced size, is not; howbig simulates those designs instead.

On-demand simulation

simulate_power() runs the pipeline above for any design in the default scenario, for the six methods whose packages it wraps, with the same network family as the grid. It was checked by re-simulating grid cells:

Design Grid Simulated (20 replicates)
InvCov, p = 100, n = 1000 0.49 0.49
JGL_BIC, p = 100, n = 1000 0.70 0.70 (± 0.02)
InvCov, p = 100, n = 500 / 1500 0.32 0.31
JGL_BIC, p = 100, n = 500 / 1500 0.62 0.61 (± 0.02)

Implementation notes:

  • Reproducible. Every replicate and permutation sets its own seed from seed, so results are identical however many cores are used.
  • Parallel-safe. Workers are separate R processes rather than forks. Forking after a multithreaded linear-algebra library (such as Apple Accelerate) has started can crash the workers.
  • Runtime estimates come from a per-method regression of log fit time on log(p) and log(n), fit to the production timings.

Source

The simulation design, generators, and scoring are ported from the simulation study for the DiNA differential network analysis tutorial (manuscript in preparation), whose main reporting family is the Barabási-Albert tree networks used as the default here.

Danaher, P., Wang, P., & Witten, D. M. (2014). The joint graphical lasso for inverse covariance estimation across multiple classes. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 76(2), 373-397.
